doc.title: Kenny Burrell — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: New York sessions, studio work and Midnight Blue
title: Recording with James Brown on Try Me
summary: Burrell recalls James Brown singing each part and demanding specific rhythms and sound at the 1958 session.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"

blocks.x: Sure, well, I do want to go back to that period between Introducing Kenny Burrell, ’56, and lets say Midnight Blue, which is…
I’ve got a class at five…
Okay. [laughs] No problem.
I’m sorry. [laughs]
People recognize universally and that’s the one you did with Coltrane…
Right.
And the other is from that same year, from ’58, that you did with the Godfather of Soul that most people probably aren’t aware of, of “Try Me”. Do you remember that session?

I remember being there, I remember being there, I don’t remember dates. I mean, the tracks and all, but I remember interacting with him. Yeah, are we, yeah, we’re recording. I remembering James Brown being really specific for every instrument and every person about what he wanted them to play, and I was so happy I could meet his satisfaction because I didn’t want to disappoint him. I mean, again, I love all kinds of music and respected him tremendously and this is part of my stuff as a studio musician. And I got the call and I said, “Sure.” But he had specific, particularly rhythms, he had rhythms that he wanted you to play and he had a sound that he wanted you go get out of your instrument. So I was able to somehow do it like he wanted and it was okay.
So, well, James didn’t hand out charts, obviously…
No. Brown:…so he just sang? How did he communicate?
He sang the part…
He sang the part.

He said…[sings vocal rhythms]…and so you had to try and get that and you mess around with the amp and finally he said, “Yeah, that’s, that’s”. And when you get it he said, “Okay”, and then he’d go to the next guy. There wasn’t a lot of harmonic changes there, some, but not a lot, so you didn’t have to worry about that too much. But rhythmically, and the sound and the voicing, of course, because the voicing has to do with how it’s going to sound. He knew what he wanted in his own way, you know, he was a master of that and when he put it all together it worked. Yeah, so you mentioned one track in particular.
Well, “Try Me” was the big hit. [sings] I mean, we could put it on, but…
No, I’m just saying I didn’t even know that was the big hit…
Yeah. Burrell:…that I was on.
And I think the flipside was “Tell Me What I Did Wrong.”
Okay, you know more than I do about it.
Well, you were doing so many sessions it’s amazing that you can even remember doing half of them.
But, man, that’s why I say you are the right guy for this. Man, you are something, man, that’s great, I’m so glad. Any way, yeah, so…
